Texto 3: Questões de 55 a 60
São Paulo sets record for femicide before year-end
The number of femicides in the city of São Paulo reached a record
high in 2025, even before the year has ended. According to data from
the State Public Security Secretariat, from January to October, 53 kil-
lings of women were recorded in cases where the motive was directly
classified as violence against women.
This is the highest number of crimes of this kind in the city since
2015, when data collection began following a change in the law that
created the classification of femicide for murders of women involving
domestic or family violence, or contempt for the victim’s status as a
woman.
Even without the figures for November and December, the total
already surpasses last year’s full-year record of 51 cases. Statewide,
between January and October, there have been 207 femicides in 2025,
compared with 191 in the same period of the previous year.
The rise in femicide is not unique to São Paulo. According to Ca-
rolina Ricardo, executive director of the Sou da Paz Institute, the trend
is rooted in machismo and in the misogynistic belief held by some men
that women are a form of property. This distorted perception, she says,
legitimizes violence against women in the minds of many aggressors.
“Even our legal frameworks have legitimized this violence –
whether by criminalizing adultery, which placed blame squarely on
women, or in cases involving the ‘defense of honor,’ in which men were
exempted from guilt for violence against women.”
The so-called “legitimate defense of honor” argument was com-
monly used by defense lawyers throughout the last century in cases of
violence against women, often invoking claims of jealousy or passion.
Although the principle was abolished in the 1988 Constitution, which
established equality between men and women, it was only in 2023 that
the Supreme Court (STF) formally declared the argument unconstituti-
onal and prohibited its use in any courtroom.
Ricardo adds that despite progress, increased awareness, and gre-
ater public visibility of the issue, misogyny and violence against wo-
men are being amplified online by movements driven by sexist ideas –
precisely in reaction to the social and political gains women have achi-
eved in recent years.
“We are seeing a rise in gender-based violence in a context of
growing radicalization,” she says. “There is this phenomenon of sexist
influencers, the ‘red pill’ movement, and we are starting to see violence
by boys against girls, for example. Social media accelerates this because
content spreads much faster there.”
According to the executive director of the Sou da Paz Institute,
the radicalization of violence against women is not limited to Brazil.
“It is part of a global trend,” she explains. “And it has contributed to
increasingly brutal acts, such as the recent cases we have witnessed –
women being dragged into cars, two women murdered inside a school.
These are ferocious crimes.”
